competition_series: FSAE (SAE International, North America); FSG/FS-family European series (Formula Student Germany, FS East, FS Czech, FS UK, etc.); FSAE-Australasia
summary: Testing an FSAE driverless car requires far more than track time: a private lot or closed track with a large-enough safe/runoff area, a sizeable cone inventory (competition geometry alone implies well over 100 cones per full-scale layout), a trained safety-marshalling crew empowered to hit the Remote Stop, and a staged low-speed-to-full-speed test plan that culminates in a genuinely dangerous dynamic maneuver: the Emergency Brake System (EBS) test at 40 km/h with an 8.5 m stopping requirement. Cross-team evidence shows realistic test cadences of roughly 2-3 organized sessions per week in the final competition run-up (Monash Motorsport, 2024), staged hardware-safety-first validation sequences spanning many months (UTFR: standalone EBS validation, then full-vehicle EBS, then remote-stop validation, then comprehensive system validation, then full-course autonomous navigation - a ~1-year sequence), and cases where teams had only a handful of test days on a borrowed platform before their first competition (EUFS, ~3 days on the shared ADS-DV in 2018). The single most important safety lesson in this space is QUT Motorsport's December 2024 crash: a software path-planning latency issue caused a sharp corrective steering input at 40 km/h during the live EBS test, sending the car into a wall/tyre barrier despite Remote Stop and EBS both activating - ending that car's competitive life and demonstrating that the EBS test itself, not just EBS hardware, must be built up to incrementally with adequate runoff, low-speed increments, and fault-injection testing on a stationary rig before any full-speed dynamic attempt.

year_by_year_timeline.mechanical_focus: EBS actuator/mechanism motion range, force/travel curves, mounting integrity, mechanical end-stops verified off-vehicle
year_by_year_timeline.electrical_focus: Pressure sensor calibration against known reference sources; supply voltage/current draw characterized
year_by_year_timeline.software_focus: N/A at this stage - no vehicle control loop active yet
year_by_year_timeline.milestone_achieved: A representative test stand (per FS driverless practice) captures brake pressure, actuator position, supply voltage/current, temperatures, and safety state with synchronized timestamps, enabling detection of mechanical binding or thermal issues without a moving vehicle.

year_by_year_timeline.mechanical_focus: Pressure cycling across representative brake applications; leak detection and air-bleeding; repeated-cycle behavior documented
year_by_year_timeline.electrical_focus: Pressure sensor cross-checks and calibration confirmed under real cycling
year_by_year_timeline.milestone_achieved: Both independent pneumatic/hydraulic circuits (redundancy is a hard DSF/DT.3.2 requirement) individually proven to build, hold, and release pressure as designed.

year_by_year_timeline.phase_name: Safety and fault injection on the jacked-up/stationary vehicle
year_by_year_timeline.mechanical_focus: Mechanical resistance/binding trends monitored across cycles
year_by_year_timeline.electrical_focus: Loss of LV supply, communication timeout, pressure-sensor-fault, and unintended-brake-drag scenarios deliberately injected while stationary to confirm safe-state transitions and reset procedures
year_by_year_timeline.software_focus: Watchdog/monitoring flowchart logic (per the DSF's own Continuous Monitoring and Startup Checks flowcharts) exercised against every documented failure case
year_by_year_timeline.milestone_achieved: This maps directly to the FSAE Inspection Mission (DO.1.3): vehicle supported off the ground, wheels removed, drivetrain spun slowly and steering swept in a sine pattern, transitioning to Finished after 25-30s - effectively a rehearsal for technical inspection.

year_by_year_timeline.mechanical_focus: Passive EBS path validated independently before any active/motorized system is layered on top
year_by_year_timeline.electrical_focus: Remote Stop System (Gross-Funk hardware) integration exercised at low speed with a trained Driverless System Operator (DSO) at the Control Box
year_by_year_timeline.software_focus: Perception/planning/control loop run at low speed (e.g. walking pace to ~10-20 km/h) in a controlled lot with generous runoff, tethering or spotters as an extra safety margin, well before any full-speed attempt
year_by_year_timeline.milestone_achieved: Cross-team pattern (per UTFR's documented sequence): standalone EBS validation preceded full-vehicle EBS implementation by roughly 6 months, which itself preceded remote-emergency-stop validation and a distinct 'comprehensive system validation' step before autonomous navigation testing progressed to full-course runs.

year_by_year_timeline.mechanical_focus: EBS proven at increasing speed increments, not jumped straight to the 40 km/h competition test speed
year_by_year_timeline.electrical_focus: Full shutdown-circuit chain (DSMS, RSS, EBS relay) exercised at speed with real-time monitoring
year_by_year_timeline.software_focus: Full perception-SLAM-planning-control loop run at competition-representative speeds; regular test cadence of roughly 2-3 sessions/week in the final run-up is a realistic target (per Monash Motorsport's 2024 practice, with live Foxglove telemetry monitoring and post-session rosbag replay/analysis)
year_by_year_timeline.milestone_achieved: This is the highest-risk phase and the one where QUT Motorsport's Dec 2024 crash occurred (during the competition-site EBS test itself, at 40 km/h, due to a path-planning latency fault) - underscoring that full-speed EBS testing needs a straight line with substantial marked runoff (cones similar to Acceleration layout per DI.2.2.1) well clear of any wall or barrier.

ramp_phases: Phase 0: bench/stationary component testing (actuator, pressure sensors) - days to weeks
Phase 2: stationary fault-injection testing (jacked up, wheels off, mirrors the Inspection Mission) - weeks, can run in parallel with Phase 1
Phase 3: low-speed incremental dynamic testing with generous runoff/tethering/spotters - weeks to a couple months
Phase 4: full-speed dynamic testing culminating in EBS-test-representative runs (40 km/h, 8.5m stop) - final weeks to months before competition, requires the most test-day volume
what_slipped: The clearest documented slip pattern is QUT Motorsport's: the team had a full 10-lap Trackdrive completed in pre-competition testing, yet the live on-site EBS test - immediately before their scheduled Trackdrive run - is where an unpredictable path-computation delay caused a crash, ending the car's season despite months of prior successful testing. This shows that testing volume and even competition-representative success in earlier phases does not guarantee the final, highest-stakes dynamic test (the EBS test) will go safely; that test specifically needs to be over-tested and treated as a distinct risk category, not just 'more of the same' driving. More generally across teams researched, testing-hours/testing-days figures are rarely published with precision (most teams describe cadence qualitatively - '2-3x/week', 'countless trips'), which is itself a signal that few teams instrument or report their testing volume rigorously, making before/after comparisons for new teams difficult.
platform_prerequisites: A team needs, at minimum: (1) a private or leasable lot/track large enough for a 200-500m autocross-scale layout with 3m minimum width and 9m minimum turning diameter, plus a straight section of 75-100m+ for acceleration/EBS-representative runs with substantial additional runoff beyond the competition's own 75m/8.5m stopping requirements; (2) an adequate cone inventory (see sensor/mounting-adjacent fields below); (3) a trained Driverless System Operator (DSO) and marshalling crew empowered to operate the Remote Stop Control Box and physically clear/re-enter the area per DD.3.2-DD.3.3; (4) the standardized Remote Stop System hardware (Gross-Funk Control Box + Vehicle Module) already procured and commissioned, since it is the mechanism used to safely abort every dynamic test, not just competition runs.
ebs_design: N/A - covered in the companion 'Driverless Safety Concept and Required Documentation' research item. This item focuses on how EBS testing is staged and de-risked, not the EBS architecture itself.
ebs_development_duration: [uncertain] UTFR's documented sequence gives the clearest dated proxy found: standalone EBS validation (Nov 2023) to full-vehicle EBS implementation (May 2024) was roughly 6 months, followed by remote-emergency-stop validation (Jun 2024) and a distinct 'comprehensive system validation' step (Jul 2024) - i.e., roughly 8-9 months from first standalone EBS validation to a fully validated, vehicle-integrated, remote-stop-tested system.
ebs_cost_estimate: [uncertain] No consolidated rig/test-infrastructure cost figure was found in sources reviewed. Commodity industrial pneumatics (Festo-class valves/cylinders, paintball-class certified air tanks/regulators, pressure sensors) referenced in the DSF's own example bill of materials suggest a bench test-rig instrumentation cost (pressure transducers, DAQ, timestamping) in the low thousands of USD on top of the EBS hardware itself, but this is an inference, not a sourced figure.
steering_actuation: N/A - see companion Safety Concept/Documentation item and individual team files.
brake_actuation: N/A - see EBS design note above.
shutdown_circuit_implementation: N/A - see companion Documentation item; relevant here only insofar as every dynamic test must exercise the same Remote Stop Relay / EBS Relay chain that competition will use, so test-day procedure should always include a live Remote Stop drill, not just a nominal-path run.
remote_stop_system: The Gross-Funk Control Box + Vehicle Module RSS is the single mechanism used to abort any dynamic test, including team-organized practice sessions, not just competition runs (DO.2.2.2: the RSS Control Box is the only device permitted to send commands to the vehicle during driverless operation). Teams train with a Training E-Key (distinct from the single-use Race E-Key issued only for scored competition runs); the RSS has a 200ms pre-alarm before a radio-loss-triggered shutdown, and its vehicle-module relay must sit directly in the shutdown circuit. Every test day should assign one trained DSO to hold this box at a clear, designated location per DD.3.2.1, with the rest of the team clear of the vehicle before any driverless run per the FSG Beginners Guide's procedure (leave the vehicle area, proceed to the ASR/DSO location, wait for 'AS Ready', get official approval before sending Go).
simulation_tooling: N/A - not this item's focus; note only that staged testing should begin in simulation (per multiple teams' documented practice, e.g. QUT's eufs_sim/Gazebo work before any hardware existed) prior to Phase 0 physical bench testing described above, since simulation is the cheapest and safest place to find planning/control bugs before they surface as an EBS-test failure mode like QUT's.
data_logging: Live telemetry monitoring during test sessions (e.g. Foxglove) plus post-session rosbag/log replay and analysis is documented team practice (Monash Motorsport, 2024 season) and is directly relevant to testing cadence: a 'test day' is not just track time but includes a data-review loop afterward to find issues before the next session. The DSF/RSS documentation also requires EBS pressure signals to be logged via CAN (0x500) during any run where the energy meter is connected, meaning competition-representative test days should also validate that this logging path actually works end-to-end, not just the driving behavior.
open_source_repos: https://github.com/QUT-Motorsport/QUTMS_Driverless - the mission_controller package's ebs_test.launch.py and rosbag_creator operations package are a concrete, public reference for how one team structured EBS-test-specific software missions and automated post-run data capture.
critical_path_items: 1) Physical test-site access (a private lot or closed track meeting the minimum geometry) is the single hardest infrastructure item to arrange and is not something software effort can substitute for - teams without reliable, recurring access cannot execute the staged low-to-full-speed plan described above. 2) The live EBS test specifically is the critical, irreducible final validation gate; per QUT's case, no amount of successful lower-risk testing (even a full completed Trackdrive) substitutes for dedicated, repeated, incrementally-staged EBS-maneuver testing at increasing speed. 3) A trained, available marshalling/DSO crew - the RSS-based safe-testing procedure requires dedicated personnel at every session, which is a recurring people-scheduling constraint, not a one-time setup cost.
long_lead_procurement: [uncertain] The Remote Stop System (single-source, Gross-Funk GmbH) is the clearest procurement item gating any dynamic testing at all - without a commissioned RSS, DO.2.2.2/DD rules do not permit driverless-mode operation, so this should be ordered as early as possible; no public lead-time-in-weeks figure was found, but its single-supplier nature (flagged also in the companion Documentation item) is a plausible multi-week risk for a first-time team. Cone inventory (see below) is a comparatively short-lead commodity purchase by contrast.
testing_hours_before_first_comp: [uncertain, synthesized from cross-team proxies] No team in this research set published a precise cumulative testing-hours figure. Proxies found: Monash Motorsport ran organized test sessions 2-3 times per week in the lead-up to their 2024 European campaign; UTFR's UT25 completed 200+ km of general vehicle testing within 19 days of its March 2025 unveiling (not driverless-specific, but indicative of test-day intensity achievable with focused effort); Edinburgh (EUFS) had only ~3 days of familiarization on a shared/borrowed ADS-DV platform before FSUK 2018, illustrating the low end of the range for teams not testing their own build. A reasonable planning estimate synthesized from these data points for a team building and testing its own vehicle: at least 15-25 dedicated dynamic test days (2-3 sessions/week for the final 2-3 months) before a first competition entry, with additional bench/stationary Phase 0-2 testing time on top not counted in that day figure.
validation_strategy: The consistent, repeated pattern across teams researched is staged mission-based validation that mirrors the competition's own event structure: an Inspection Mission (stationary, wheels off, sine-wave steering sweep) as the lowest-risk rehearsal; a dedicated EBS-test mission run repeatedly and separately from normal driving missions; and full-course/Trackdrive-equivalent missions only attempted once the lower-risk missions are solid (QUT's mission_controller package implements exactly this: inspection.launch.py, ebs_test.launch.py, trackdrive.launch.py as distinct, separately-tunable software missions). The openelab.io EBS validation guide formalizes this further into 4 phases: bench/mechanism testing, hydraulic/pneumatic system testing, safety/fault-injection testing (stationary), and only then vehicle-level dynamic validation - explicitly warning against 'introducing multiple untested systems simultaneously on a moving vehicle' and cautioning that motor torque-curve specs alone do not prove vehicle-level EBS compliance, since linkage play, hydraulic compliance, sensor lag, and spring preload all contribute to real-world stopping performance.
rules_compliance_challenges: N/A - see companion Documentation item for rules-compliance content; this item's focus is testing execution, not rules text.
ebs_test_experience: QUT Motorsport (Dec 2024, FSAE-A) is the critical cautionary case for this entire research item: during the live, on-site Emergency Brake System Test - performed after other technical inspection was complete, in a straight line marked with cones similar to Acceleration, immediately before the team's scheduled Trackdrive run - an unpredictable delay in the vehicle's path-planning computation caused a sharp corrective steering input at 40 km/h just meters before the finish line, sending the car (QEV-3D) off the marked line into a nearby wall and tyre barrier. The Remote Stop and Emergency Brake System were both triggered before the car left the track, reducing impact speed, but there was not enough time to fully stop; damage was confined to a single corner's suspension (no structural, tractive, or electronic components affected), but it was enough to retire QEV-3D from competitive use - the team maintained it only as an autonomous testbed afterward while developing a next-generation platform. The direct lesson for any team about to attempt this test for the first time: (1) the EBS test's own required approach (>=40 km/h reached within 20 m) is a genuinely high-consequence maneuver, not a formality; (2) it must be preceded by extensive stationary fault-injection and low-speed incremental testing (per the openelab.io 4-phase methodology) specifically targeting planning/control latency under realistic sensor conditions, not just EBS actuator hardware function; (3) the physical test venue must have generous, unobstructed runoff well beyond the rules-minimum 8.5 m stopping distance - proximity to a wall/tyre barrier at the finish line removed QUT's margin for a software-timing fault that hardware itself did not cause; (4) teams should specifically rehearse the EBS-test speed profile (accelerate to 40 km/h, trigger stop) many times at their own test site before attempting it at competition, since QUT's failure was in the planning/control software's behavior at that specific speed and maneuver, not a novel condition unique to the competition venue.
documentation_burden: N/A - see companion 'Driverless Safety Concept and Required Documentation' research item, which covers this in full.
autonomous_speeds_achieved: The competition's own EBS test defines a concrete, universal target speed: >=40 km/h reached within a 20 m run-up (DI.2.2.2, 2026 rules). QUT's crash occurred at exactly this speed. Skidpad/Acceleration/Autocross events do not mandate a minimum speed but reward lap-time performance; team-reported cruise/control-tuning speeds seen elsewhere in this research project's team files (e.g. an ~8 m/s / ~29 km/h regulated-pure-pursuit parameter used in one team's carpark testing) are well below the 40 km/h EBS-test speed, underscoring that EBS-test-representative testing is a distinct, higher-speed regime a team must deliberately build up to rather than one that falls out naturally from lower-speed autocross practice.
ebs_deceleration_achieved: Rules requirement (see companion Documentation item for full detail): DT.3.2.5.b requires average deceleration >10 m/s2 (2026 rules; an earlier ruleset cited by a 2018 KTH thesis required >8 m/s2), with a stop required within 8.5 m from >=40 km/h and a maximum 200 ms system reaction time. No team-measured deceleration figure (as distinct from the rules requirement) was found in sources reviewed for this item.
reliability_notes: QUT Motorsport's Dec 2024 crash (detailed under ebs_test_experience) is this item's central reliability finding: an off-course/crash event during the highest-stakes dynamic test, caused by a path-planning computation delay rather than a mechanical or EBS-hardware failure, resulting in a wall/tyre-barrier strike at 40 km/h and minor single-corner suspension damage. It is the clearest publicly-documented example in this research project of a driverless test-day incident with real vehicle damage, and is the strongest available evidence for why a staged, incremental, well-instrumented EBS-test buildup (not a single full-speed attempt) is essential.
top_mistakes: 1) Under-resourcing the full 4-phase EBS validation methodology (bench -> circuit -> fault-injection -> vehicle-dynamic) and moving too quickly to full-speed dynamic testing without first exhausting stationary fault-injection scenarios (loss of LV supply, comms timeout, sensor faults) - the openelab.io guide's core warning. 2) Testing the EBS-representative maneuver for the first time at competition rather than repeatedly at the team's own test site beforehand - QUT's failure mode (planning/control latency at 40 km/h) is exactly the kind of issue that repeated, instrumented practice at that specific speed and maneuver would be expected to surface earlier and more safely. 3) Choosing or accepting a test/competition venue where the EBS-test straight has insufficient runoff beyond the rules-minimum stopping distance, removing safety margin for a fault the hardware itself did not cause. 4) Treating testing cadence as ad hoc rather than a scheduled, resourced, telemetry-reviewed cycle - teams with a documented '2-3x/week plus post-session data review' cadence (Monash) present a more mature, repeatable practice than teams relying on occasional or opportunistic access.
advice_for_new_teams: Synthesized from the sources reviewed: build a stationary test rig first and capture pressure, actuator position, supply voltage/current, temperature, and safety state with synchronized timestamps before any vehicle testing (openelab.io); validate the passive EBS mechanism completely independently of the motorized/active braking path, since 'a fast motor spec' does not prove vehicle-level EBS compliance once linkage play, hydraulic compliance, sensor lag, and spring preload are accounted for; perform fault-injection testing only while the vehicle is stationary or in a controlled, approved state, and document mechanical inspection/reset procedures after every such event; and, per the FSG Beginners Guide, design the EBS to be quickly re-armable so the team can run 'multiple EBS tests in a row' during practice, since repetition at the actual competition speed and maneuver profile is the best available defense against a QUT-style latency failure.
team_structure_dv: N/A - see companion Documentation item and individual team files; relevant here only in that a marshalling/DSO role must be staffed for every test session, not just competition days, since the same RSS-based safety procedure applies to team-run practice.
recruiting_and_knowledge_transfer: [uncertain] Not specifically documented for testing infrastructure/cadence in sources reviewed for this item.
budget_estimate: [uncertain] No consolidated testing-infrastructure budget (lot/track access fees, cone inventory, rig instrumentation) was found. The cone inventory alone, sized to the competition's own geometry minimums (skidpad's confirmed 17 pylons per inner circle x2, plus autocross/acceleration boundary marking over 75-500m courses), plausibly requires on the order of 150-300+ cones for a full-scale practice layout matching competition dimensions - a commodity purchase (standard FSAE small/large cones, 228mm/285mm per the rules) typically costing on the order of a few thousand USD depending on cone size/supplier, though no team-published purchase figure was located to confirm this range; flagged as [uncertain].
recommended_sequence: 1) Secure recurring access to a private lot/closed track meeting minimum geometry (200-500m for autocross-scale layouts, 3m min width, 75-100m+ straight with generous runoff for acceleration/EBS-representative work) before hardware is even finished, since site access is the least software-substitutable critical path item. 2) Commission the Remote Stop System and train a DSO/marshalling crew early, since it gates all driverless-mode testing, not just competition. 3) Build a stationary EBS bench rig (Phase 0) and complete circuit-level (Phase 1) and stationary fault-injection (Phase 2) testing before any vehicle leaves the ground under its own power in driverless mode. 4) Progress to low-speed incremental dynamic testing (Phase 3) with tethering/spotters and wide runoff, only escalating speed once each increment is clean. 5) Reserve full-speed, EBS-test-representative testing (Phase 4, 40 km/h) for a mature system, and run it repeatedly at the team's own site - not for the first time at competition - specifically targeting the planning/control latency failure mode that ended QUT's 2024 season. 6) Institute a fixed weekly test cadence (2-3 sessions/week in the final competition run-up, per Monash's documented practice) with a telemetry-review loop (live monitoring plus post-session log replay) after every session.
applicability_to_24_month_ramp: Highly applicable. A team with a running EV and ~9 software-focused members over 24 months (June 2026-June 2028) should explicitly budget the 4-phase EBS validation methodology and the full stationary-to-full-speed staging described above as its own tracked workstream, not something that happens implicitly as 'general testing.' Given the team is software-heavy, it should be well-positioned to build the instrumentation, telemetry, and mission-based test-launch structure (mirroring QUT's inspection/ebs_test/trackdrive mission separation) that mature teams use, but must not let software capability create false confidence about the EBS test specifically - QUT's crash happened to a team with 3+ years of development experience and a working full-course autonomous stack. The team should plan for roughly 15-25+ dedicated dynamic test days in the final 2-3 months before its first competition entry (synthesized range, see testing_hours_before_first_comp), secure test-site access and RSS hardware in the first several months of the program (not late), and treat the live EBS test as requiring dozens of repeated low-to-full-speed rehearsals at its own site before ever attempting it at a competition venue.
